"Wherefore," he says, i.e., because of what is to come, because of the good things that are laid up in store for them who rightly believe and live. And it is meet then to give thanks to God both for all the things which mankind have received at His hands, both heretofore and hereafter; and meet to give Him thanks also for the faith of them that believe.

"Having heard," saith he, "of the faith in the Lord Jesus which is among you, and which ye show toward all the saints." […]

Therefore I also, hearing of your faith in the Lord Jesus, and toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, making remembrance of you in my prayers: that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him, the eyes of your heart enlightened.

Although a translation rendered word for word could excuse the Apostle to the diligent reader, in that the whole connection of the sentence seems to teem with faults and a solecism results, yet in the Greek too it sounds like a fault. Hence we also, answering rather the Greek detractors, will try to adjust the order of the reading according to the sense, so that we say: Hearing of your faith in the Lord Jesus, and toward all his saints, and seeing the difference of your faith toward the Lord and toward all his saints, I do not cease to give thanks and to make remembrance of you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, but the Father of glory, may give you the spirit of […]

"Having heard," he says, "of your faith in Christ Jesus." And not only of faith, but also of love, that is, a merciful and brotherly disposition, and even a philanthropic one, as extending to all and not only to the local saints, that is, to the poor among the believers. And everywhere he joins love with faith, since it gives birth to a virtuous life. For without it faith is useless — faith without works and life; just as life is also useless without faith.

1:16.t:
"For this reason." Why then? Because you, having believed, received the seal of the Spirit and obtained the pledge of future blessings and perfect redemption, and are to receive what has been prepared for those who rightly believe and live piously — "I unceasingly give thanks for you." Do you see what a compassionate heart? He offers thanksgiving for all, as if he himself had received the benefit. For he writes this not only to the Ephesians, but to all. So then, although it is worthy to thank God for all else that we have been deemed worthy of, it is also worthy to give thanks for the faith of the believers, because they were so enlightened that they fled to the cross of the Savior, turning away from the destroyer. For such is the nature of brotherly love.

Note how many he has in his mind, how many he remembered in his prayers. But we do not even remember ourselves as we ought.

1:17.t: From Him also is besought "the spirit of wisdom," at whose disposal is enumerated that sevenfold distribution of the spirit of grace by Isaiah.

Moreover, when the apostle in his epistle prays, "That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and of knowledge," He must be other (than Christ), who is the God of Jesus Christ, the bestower of spiritual gifts.

If the Father is father of something that subsists and is substantial, and he is called also the Father of glory, then plainly glory is something that subsists and is given substance; and perhaps our Savior, just as he is "the Word" and "Wisdom" and "Truth" and "Peace" and "Righteousness", so also is "Glory"; and if ever it is recorded that the "Glory" of God was seen, we must understand nothing else to have been seen than the Son of God.

Now the spirit of wisdom makes one wise, while the spirit of revelation takes away the veil from the heart, so that one, "with unveiled face beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, is transformed into the same image from glory to glory". No one, then, who is not wise has a spirit of wisdom, and no one of those who still have, "whenever Moses is read, a veil upon the heart", has yet received the spirit of revelation; unless indeed the spirit of wisdom makes people wise in differing degrees according to the quantity of the contemplations of wisdom, and, according to the quantity of the removal of the veils that lie upon the letters, it administers the revelation not in like manner to those from whom the veil is removed.

All this the Apostle confirms in one short and decisive sentence, Making mention of you in my prayers that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give unto you a spirit of wisdom and revelation. When he speaks of Him as Jesus Christ, he mentions His God: when his theme is the glory of Christ, he calls God His Father. To Christ, as having glory, God is Father: to Christ, as being Jesus, God is God. ... Where the glory of Christ is concerned, God is His Father; where Christ is Jesus, there the Father is His God. In the Dispensation by which He is a servant, He has as God Him Whom, in the glory by which He is God, He has as Father.

Yet he calls God the Father of glory, and the God of Christ, although God is the true Father of Christ, and the God of creation. But the Lord himself too says the same: I go to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God (John 20:17). He is therefore the Father of all glory, because from him is all glory, and power, and dignity. He is also the Father of Christ, but in another way, because this one is the true Son, and he is the God of all, but he is not the God of Christ in the same way. For he is the God of Christ in this way: because Christ is God from God; but to the rest he is God as a cause of fear, as he himself says in Malachi the prophet: If I am God, where is my fear (Mal. 1:6)?

As to the other passages, My God would be used in respect, not of the Word, but of the Visible Word. For how could there be a God of Him Who is properly God? In the same way He is Father, not of the Visible, but of the Word; for our Lord was of two Natures; so that one expression is used properly, the other improperly in each of the two cases; but exactly the opposite way to their use in respect of us. For with respect to us God is properly our God, but not properly our Father. And this is the cause of the error of the Heretics, namely the joining of these two Names, which are interchanged because of the Union of the Natures. And an indication of this is found in the fact that wherever the Natures are distinguished in our thoughts from one another, the Names are also distinguished; as you hear in Paul's words, "The God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of Glory." The God of Christ, but the Father of glory. […]

What is thy prayer, and what thy entreaty? It is "That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give unto you a spirit of wisdom and revelation." Two things he requires them to understand, as it is their duty to understand them; to what blessings they are called, and how they have been released from their former state. He says, however, himself, that these points are three. How then are they three? In order that we may understand touching the things to come; for from the good things laid up for us, we shall know His ineffable and surpassing riches, and from understanding who we were, and how we believed, we shall know His power and sovereignty, in turning again to Himself those who had been so long time estranged from Him, "For the weakness of God is stronger than men." Inasmuch as it is by the self-same power by which He raised Christ from the dead, that He hath also drawn us to Himself. Nor is that power limited to the resurrection, but far exceeds it. […]

He is the witness of all that the Father promised and bestowed on the world, whose mystery Paul gathers up in a brief word to the Ephesians: The God, he says, of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory (Eph 1:17); of whom it is written now as well: Because of the Lord your God, and the Holy One of Israel, who has glorified you, and that with the glory which He had before the world was made. Of it the Prophet also testifies: The glory of God shall appear (Heb 1), He who is the brightness of glory and the form of His substance, when every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of the Father (Phil 2). He answered the Son, when He asked for the glory which He had had before: I have both glorified it, and will glorify it. Of which the apostle John also says: We saw, he says, His glory, the glory as of the only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth (John 12:28; 1:14). Therefore, when he speaks of Him who in the beginning was with God, God the Word, He is called the Father of glory; […]

Further, the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, but the Father of glory, is to be understood thus: that just as our Lord Jesus Christ is himself the word, wisdom, truth, peace, righteousness, fortitude, so he is also glory, according to what is said elsewhere: The glory of God shall appear (Lev. 9:23); and in nearly the whole of the old Law it is written that the glory of God was seen above the tabernacle of the testimony (Num. 9). And the Psalmist sings: Arise, my glory, arise (Ps. 107:3). This glory, enlightening the world with its brightness, built itself a temple from the virginal womb. Of that temple the Father of glory becomes the God. And where Christ is glory, there he is called only Father; where he is Jesus, there the Father is named his God, without any addition. This, then, the God of the man assumed, but the Father of glory, of wisdom, of truth, gives to those who believe in his Son the spirit of wisdom and of revelation, that they may become wise, and with unveiled face may contemplate the glory of the Lord.

And as for what he says, in the knowledge of him, that is, ἐπιγνώσει αὐτοῦ, some understand it thus, that between γνῶσιν and ἐπίγνωσιν, that is, between knowing (notio) and knowledge (agnitio), the difference is this: that knowing (notio) is of things which we did not know before and afterwards began to know; but knowledge (agnitio) is of things which, having known them before, we then ceased to know, and afterwards recall; and they surmise a certain former life in the heavenly places, in that, having been cast down into these bodies and having forgotten God the Father, we have now come to know him through revelation, according to that word: All the ends of the earth shall remember and shall turn to the Lord (Ps. 21:28), unfolding other things like these.

So we understand two kinds of action in the maggenanutha granted by God unto mankind one is symbolical and intelligible; the other practical. The former is connected with the holiness which is received through divine grace; this means: by the influence of the Holy Ghost a man is made holy in body and soul, as is the case of Elisha and John and Mary the blessed among women. But because this is incomparable and above that which happens to the rank-and-file of creatures we have to come to that partial [holiness] which is granted unto the other saints, in the relation between the limbs and the body.

The mysterious kind of maggenanutha — as the [gifts] imparted unto each of the saints — is a kind of influence which possesses the mind. And when man is deemed worthy of this maggenanutha, the mind is snatched away in ecstasy and expanded by some divine revelation. And as long as the influence possesses the mind, man is exalted above the emotions of psychic deliberations, on account of his communion with the Holy Ghost. […]

What do you pray and ask for on our behalf? That God may give you wisdom — "the God" of "our Lord Jesus," that is, of the Man like us according to the flesh. "The Father of glory," that is, the One who has granted us great and glorious blessings. For he always names Him on a particular basis, as in the expression: "the Father of mercies and God of all comfort" (2 Cor. 1:3); and the prophet: "O Lord, my strength, my shield" (Ps. 18:2–3). Therefore here also, since He has granted us great and glorious blessings, he calls Him the Father of glory, that is, the source. For one cannot call Him by any other than the most glorious name we have. Gregory the Theologian, however, understood "glory" as the Divinity of the Only-Begotten; so that in relation to the same Christ, He is both God and Father: in relation to Christ, that is, to His humanity, God; and in relation to glory, that is, to His Divinity, Father.

1:18.t: He likewise will grant "the enlightenment of the eyes of the understanding," who has also enriched our natural eyes with light; to whom, moreover, the blindness of the people is offensive: "And who is blind, but my servants? .

In His gift, too, are "the riches (of the glory) of His inheritance in the saints," who promised such an inheritance in the call of the Gentiles: "Ask of me, and I will give Thee the heathen for Thine inheritance.

In addition to these things we must attend to the phrase "the eyes of the heart being enlightened in the knowledge of him"; for if knowledge of God and recognition of God are not the same, but the one who recognizes, as it were, knows again what he had known long ago and forgotten, then all who come into recognition of God knew him long ago; wherefore "all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord". And the phrase "the eyes of the heart being enlightened" discloses the incorporeal and intelligible nature of our ruling faculty and of "the true light".
The calling of God has a hope, which one must come to know from much attentiveness of life and readiness of mind; and his inheritance has a wealth of much glory in the saints, in the places above.

He to whom, according to Paul's prayer, the spirit of wisdom and of revelation is given, that man will know the things "laid up" for those who are called, and will behold the things hoped for, which are the wealth of glory pertaining to his inheritance, which he gives to those who are called to this holy inheritance.

You will inquire whether God himself too is the inheritance of the saints, so that the heirs of God are understood also in this sense, in order that, just as we speak of heirs of estates and heirs of houses, ranging the inheritance under the head of possessions, so we may understand also the heirs of God. And of just such a sense is the law that says "But to the sons of Levi you shall not give a portion in the midst of their brothers, for I am their portion, says the Lord," and elsewhere "The Lord is their inheritance."

For he who by the outward eyes was not able to see the Lord in His signs, he when those bodily eyes were closed, saw with those within. And because he had received the proof in his own person, he wrote to those who had their bodily eyes full of light—May He illumine the eyes of your hearts. Therefore the signs manifested to the external eyes of the Jews, profited them not at all; but faith of the heart opened the eyes of the heart of the Gentiles.

That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him, to have the eyes of your heart enlightened, to this end, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the inheritance of his glory in the saints. It is plain that he says he prays for them for this reason: that they may know the hope of their faith in the heavenly reward; because when they fully know what the fruit of believers is, they will become more eager to cultivate religion. For it seems that there will already be progress of this kind, because if they are so devout before they know the glory of the promise, they will necessarily become more eager when they have come to know it.

"Having the eyes of your heart enlightened in the knowledge of Him."

He that hath learned what God is, will have no misgiving about His promises, and disbelief about what hath been already brought to pass. He prays, then, that there may be given them "a spirit of wisdom and revelation." Yet still he also establishes it, as far as he can himself, by arguments, and from "already" existing facts. For, whereas he was about to mention some things which had already come to pass, and others which had not as yet happened; he makes those which have been brought to pass, a pledge of those which have not: in some such way, I mean, as this,

"That ye may know," saith he, "what is the hope of His calling."

It is as yet, he means, hidden, but not so to the faithful.

"And," again, "what is the riches of the glory of His inheritance in the saints."

This too is as yet hidden.

"The riches of the glory,"

That is, the unutterable glory; […]

And when this wisdom and revelation have made them wise and have opened to them the hidden mysteries, it follows at once that they have the eyes of the heart enlightened. From the present words it is proved that, corresponding to the members of the outer man, members of the inner man are also spoken of. For see, he has plainly named the eyes of the heart, which we cannot understand apart from the sense and the mind. With this agrees also that word of the Psalmist: Enlighten my eyes, that I may never sleep in death (Ps. 12:4). And elsewhere: The eyes of the wise man are in his head (Eccles. 2:14). For if we take them simply as the eyes of the flesh, surely the eyes not only of the wise man but also of the fool are in his head. So the head of the wise man is taken to be the sense, which by another word is called the mind (mens), and the mind (animus), and the ruling part of the heart.

Now the inheritance is to be understood in two ways: either that the Firstborn of all creation is the inheritance of the soul of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the man who was assumed from body and soul, and that we, together with the inheritance of the soul, inherit God the Word; or that our inheritance in Christ is the one divinity of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; so that, just as the very things which are possessed by heirs are called an inheritance of houses and country estates, so God himself is the inheritance of believers and of the saints. It is written also in the Old Testament: But to the sons of Levi you shall not give an inheritance in the midst of their brothers, for I am their portion (Num. 18:20); and elsewhere: The Lord is their inheritance (Deut. 18:2); and the saint who knows that he has nothing outside God boldly says: My portion is the Lord (Ps. 72:26); and: You are the portion of my inheritance and of my cup (Ps. 15:5).

That you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, and what the sublime greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of the might of his power, which he wrought in Christ, raising him from the dead.

He to whom, according to Paul's prayer, the spirit of wisdom and of revelation has once been given, so that he looks with the eyes of the heart opened, will know what things are laid up for those who are called, and what the saints of God are to hope for, things which he will give abundantly and generously to those who await his inheritance. For this knowledge the greatness of the power of God is necessary in those who, after the likeness of Paul, are called believers, the power through which God wrought in Christ Jesus, whom he raised again from the dead.

It is therefore a matter of no small study that we should know the hope of the calling and the riches of the glory of God's inheritance in the saints; for to come to know these things we need that power which God also used in raising his Son: whom he raised from the dead not once but always, and made him free among the dead, stained by no contagion of death. Daily Christ rises from the dead; daily he is raised again in those who repent. Not that he did not have, even according to the flesh, the power to lay down his soul and to take it up again (for no one takes it away, unless he lays it down of himself), but in the sense that, according to the dispensation of the flesh and of the son, the man and Son is said to have been raised by God and the Father.

That is, that He may give you the gift of being enlightened by the Spirit. For if the Spirit does not reveal the hidden mysteries, it is impossible to comprehend them by any other means. For only "He," and not an angel nor an archangel, "searches all things, even the deep things of God" (1 Cor. 2:10). "The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God" (1 Cor. 2:14). Therefore, when the Spirit reveals the mysteries to us, then we shall be in the knowledge of God, and our eyes shall be enlightened, and we shall not doubt and say that this or that is impossible, but shall see all things as they are.

That is, to what hope we are called. It is clear that it is to adoption and to the enjoyment of heavenly blessings and to having Christ as our head. But since this belongs to the future, spiritual revelation is needed to know it.

And this, as something still unknown, has need of revelation from the Spirit — namely, what blessings the saints will inherit. For they are great. […]

In the beginning I call upon the first principle, from whom all illuminations descend as from the Father of lights, from whom is every good gift and every perfect gift, namely the eternal Father, through his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, that by the intercession of the most holy Virgin Mary, mother of the same God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and of blessed Francis, our leader and father, he may give the enlightened eyes of our mind to direct our feet in the way of that peace which surpasses all understanding; which peace our Lord Jesus Christ proclaimed and gave.

1:19.t: It was He who "wrought in Christ His mighty power, by raising Him from the dead, and setting Him at His own right hand, and putting all things under His feet" -even the same who said: "Sit Thou on my right hand, until I make Thine enemies Thy footstool.

The wealth of the glory of the inheritance of God, then, comes to be in the mind of the saints; since they will contain such great things of the contemplation of God and of his Word by the surpassing greatness of the power of God that is toward the saints and those who believe. For we have need not of some ordinary power from God for the knowing of what is the hope of his calling and what is the wealth of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, but of a greatness of his power coming to be in us who believe, coming from him, and coming according to the working of his strength that prevails over all things, which is now named by Paul the might of his strength; and it was by employing this working of the might of his strength that he wrought the things he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead.

And what is the exceeding greatness of his power toward you who believe, according to the working of the might of his strength, which he wrought in Christ, raising him from the dead, and he set him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every Principality and Power, and Virtue, and Dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. He declares that the pattern of the salvation and glory of believers consists in the resurrection of the Savior, so that from it the faithful may know what has been promised to them. For in like manner they will be raised above the heavens, to be with Christ; as he himself says: Father, I will that where I shall be, these also may be with me, and may see my glory (John 17:24). This is on account of the incarnation of the Son of God, so that even having been made man he may be said to be above all the heavens, and above the whole creation, sitting at the right hand of God, having the name of God by nature, not by adoption; […]

But what is clear? that through His power we have believed that He hath raised Christ. For to persuade souls, is a thing far more miraculous than to raise a dead body. I will endeavor to make this clear. Hearken then. Christ said to the dead, "Lazarus, come forth," and straightway he obeyed. Peter said, "Tabitha, arise," and she did not refuse. He Himself shall speak the word at the last day, and all shall rise, and that so quickly, that "they which are yet alive, shall in no wise precede them that are fallen asleep," and all shall come to pass, all run together "in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye." But in the matter of believing, it is not thus, but how is it? Hearken then to Him again, how He saith, "How often would I have gathered thy children together, and ye would not." You perceive that this last is the more difficult. Accordingly, it is upon this that he builds up the whole argument; because by human calculations it is far more difficult to influence the choice, than to work upon nature. […]

Since he was speaking within the limits of human language and was unable to hymn the Lord as he wished and show the greatness of his gifts, the holy apostle brings together many things under one name, striving to reveal these as much as language permits. The name "Father of glory" embraces the hope of our calling and the riches of the glory of our inheritance, the exceeding greatness of his power and the good pleasure of his will, and all that goes with it. But "the immeasurable greatness of his power" ironically now comes to mind as he thinks of the dishonor of the cross and considers how much was achieved through it.
1:19.s: Interpretation of the Epistle to the Ephesians 1.19

1:19.t: The foregoing concerned the future. But now he speaks of what has already taken place, so that from this the former might also become credible. What then is this? That, he says, we believed, for this too requires revelation, so that you might understand it more clearly. So then what? Did the Ephesians not realize that they had believed? Of course they realized it, but not in the way he now speaks of. For it is not easy to know this, because great power is needed to persuade a soul and turn it away from error — such power is needed as is not required for raising the dead. For the Lord raised the dead by a single word alone, yet He did not persuade the Jews even with many speeches and wondrous deeds. Therefore he says that for this too we have need of the revelation of the Spirit, in order to understand that our acceptance of faith is a matter of great power and the working of God. And just as He raised Christ from the dead, so also He raised us, who were dead, from unbelief. […]

1:20.t: We must hold that these things are said with a bodily figure, not as though there were certain perceptible seats or thrones set in the heavens, on which the Father sits, and the Son at the right hand of the Father; for if we understand them thus, we would not be speaking of these things worthily of the divine nature. For not even to God himself is "the earth" subjected in a bodily way, as he sits in heaven, as "the footstool of his feet". For how can "heaven be a throne", being measured by his span? And "the earth the footstool of his feet", when it too is enclosed within his fist? For Isaiah says, "Who measured the water with his hand, and heaven with a span, and all the earth with his fist?" […]

We cannot be ignorant that the Lord Jesus Christ rose again from the dead, and sits at the right hand of God, for we have also the witness of the Apostle, According to the working of the strength of His might, which He wrought in Christ, when He raised Him from the dead, and made Him to sit at His right hand in the heavenly places above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and every name that is named not only in this world but also in that which is to come, and put all things in subjection under His feet. The language of the Apostle, as befits the power of God, speaks of the future as already past: for that which is to be wrought by the completion of time already exists in Christ, in Whom is all fulness, and `future' refers only to the temporal order of the Dispensation, not to a new development. Thus, God has put all things under His feet, though they are still to be subjected. […]

Seest thou how great things He hath wrought? He hath raised up Christ. Is this a small thing? But look again. He hath set Him at His right hand. And shall any language then be able to represent this? Him that is of the earth, more mute than the fishes, and made the sport of devils, He hath in a moment raised up on high. Truly this is indeed the "exceeding greatness of His power." And behold, whither He hath raised Him.

"In the heavenly places;"

He hath made Him far above all created nature, far above all rule and authority.

And making him sit at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion, and every name that is named not only in this age but also in the age to come.

Through a human likeness he has shown the might of God: not that a throne is set up, and God the Father sits on it and has the Son sitting with him; but because we cannot understand him as judging and reigning otherwise than through our own words. To this belongs also what is written in the hundred and ninth psalm: The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet (Ps. 109:1). For if the Son sits at the Father's right hand in the manner of one who reigns, it necessarily follows, according to the same likeness, that he is greater than the one who has sat down on the left side. […]

It is clear that he says all this of Christ in his humanity. This is what inspires wonder. For it would hardly be remarkable to say that God sits by God if fellowship in power is a corollary of their identity of nature as Father and Son. But that the human nature assumed from us should partake of the same honor as the one who assumed him, so that no difference in worship is apparent, so that the invisible Godhead is worshiped through the visible human nature—this exceeds all wonder! The holy apostle is overwhelmed. He first sings of the exceeding greatness of his power. Then he speaks of the working of his mighty strength. Then he looks for whatever he can say that might point to the extraordinary nature of his exaltation.
1:20.s: Interpretation of the Epistle to the Ephesians 1.20

1:20.t: And the words "He worked in Christ," understand them as spoken of the human nature. For the One who rose from the dead is Man, even though He was united with God.

1:21.t: To these persons one may with justice say (as Scripture itself suggests), To what distance above God do ye lift up your imaginations, O ye rashly elated men? Ye have heard "that the heavens are meted out in the palm of [His] hand:" tell me the measure, and recount the endless multitude of cubits, explain to me the fulness, the breadth, the length, the height, the beginning and end of the measurement,-things which the heart of man understands not, neither does it comprehend them. For the heavenly treasuries are indeed great: God cannot be measured in the heart, and incomprehensible is He in the mind; He who holds the earth in the hollow of His hand. Who perceives the measure of His right hand? Who knoweth His finger? Or who doth understand His hand,-that hand which measures immensity; that hand which, by its own measure, spreads out the measure of the heavens, and which comprises in its hollow the earth with the abysses; […]

Wherefore he who had received the apostolate to the Gentiles, did labour more than those who preached the Son of God among them of the circumcision. For they were assisted by the Scriptures, which the Lord confirmed and fulfilled, in coming such as He had been announced; but here, [in the case of the Gentiles,] there was a certain foreign erudition, and a new doctrine [to be received, namely], that the gods of the nations not only were no gods at all, but even the idols of demons; and that there is one God, who is "above all principality, and dominion, and power, and every name which is named;" and that His Word, invisible by nature, was made palpable and visible among men, and did descend "to death, even the death of the cross;" also, that they who believe in Him shall be incorruptible and not subject to suffering, and shall receive the kingdom of heaven.

Since, therefore, it was requisite, he says, that we should be revealed as the children of God, in expectation of whose manifestation, he says, the creation habitually groans and travails in pain, the Gospel came into the world, and passed through every Principality, and Power, and Dominion, and every Name that is named.
1:21.s: Hippolytus Refutation of All Heresies Book VII

1:21.t: Many, then, are the things that rule and lead those who need his oversight, and many are the things that exercise authority, and many the things that exercise dominion, and many too the things that impart their own power, some being effective in this age, some also in the age to come; but none of these rules a rule as great as the Son does. For all the things that rule need him as their ruler; and indeed authorities will exercise authority better when they are under the authority of Christ, since the power of God surpasses all the rest of power; and even if someone is led into a profitable servitude by those who exercise dominion well, it is necessary that these things which exercise dominion, receiving the knowledge of how to exercise dominion from the "Lord of those who exercise dominion", exercise dominion over those over whom they do. […]
For the mountains are to be explained by the heavens, and the ninety and nine sheep by the principalities and powers

"Far above all rule," he saith.

Need then indeed is there of the Spirit, of an understanding wise in the knowledge of Him. Need then is there indeed of revelation. Reflect, how vast is the distance between the nature of man and of God. Yet from this vile estate hath He exalted Him to that high dignity. Nor does He mount by degrees, first one step, then another, then a third. Amazing! He does not simply say, "above," but, "far above;" for God is above those powers which are above. And thither then hath He raised Him, Him that is one of us, brought Him from the lowest point to the supremest sovereignty, to that beyond which there is no other honor. Above "all" principality, he says, not, i.e., over one and not over another, but over all,

"Rule and authority and power, and dominion, and every name that is named."

Whatever there be in Heaven, He has become above all. And this is said of Him that was raised from the dead which is worthy of our admiration; […]

After this it is asked how what follows can be understood: above every principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. And indeed concerning the right and left hands, and concerning the sitting, we have already spoken. Now we must ask where the Apostle found these four names written, I mean principality, and power, virtue, and dominion, and from where he brought them forth into the open. For it is not right to think that one who had been instructed in the divine reading said anything that is not found in the holy books. I think, therefore, that either he brought forth into the open from the traditions of the Hebrews things that are secret, or at least, since he understood that the law is spiritual, he took in a loftier sense the things that are written as though according to history, and recognized in what is related in Numbers and in the books of Kingdoms about kings and princes, and also leaders, tribunes and centurions, an image of […]

We have said there are nine orders of angels, because we know from the testimony of sacred Scripture that there are angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominations, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim. For nearly all pages of sacred Scripture testify that there are angels and archangels. The books of the prophets frequently speak, as is well known, of cherubim and seraphim. The apostle Paul also enumerates the names of four orders to the Ephesians, saying: "Above every principality, and power, and virtue, and domination." Writing again to the Colossians, he says: "Whether thrones, or powers, or principalities, or dominations." He had already described dominations, principalities, and powers when speaking to the Ephesians; but when about to say these things also to the Colossians, he added thrones, about which he had not yet said anything to the Ephesians. […]

He did not say "high," but "far above," to indicate the greatest height. For from the uttermost depth He raised human nature in Christ to the very highest point. Of course, he speaks of it as having died and been raised, since the divine nature truly did not die, was not raised, and was not exalted, as it was always above every height. Thus, above every angelic power sat the formerly despised human nature.

Whatever it may be, he says, in heaven, it is below This One who was assumed and ascended, and He is above all. From this we learn that there are certain powers which we cannot even name now, but which will then be revealed.

1:22.t: But how it is said also that he subjected all things under his feet must be examined, since it is evident that there are countless multitudes who still do not submit to the Word of God. For "we do not yet see all things subjected"; and the saying "for he must reign until he puts all his enemies under his feet" makes clear that not yet are all the enemies under his feet. One person, then, will say that this too is said according to foreknowledge. But another, presenting the classification of God, by which he classes each into some rank, will say this: he subjected all things under his feet—as many as are of the rank of those who are subjected.

Finding the Church called the body of Christ, we inquire whether we must understand it, as the rest of the body in relation to the head, to be an instrument of the head; or whether, just as a man has a body, of which body the head is a part, so the whole Church of Christ is the body of Christ, animated by his divinity and filled by his Spirit; or whether these things must be taken in some other way. If, however, the second is the case, then the more human part of him will itself also be a part of the whole body, while the divine part, which gives life to the whole Church, will be the divine power that, as it were, animates it.

But how the Church, being the body of Christ, is the fullness of him who is filled, all in all, we wish to know, and why it is not said 'of him who fills all in all' but 'of him who is filled.' For it will seem more consistent to have said that Christ is the one who fills, and not the one who is filled; for he himself is the fullness not only "of the law", but is also the fullness of all fullnesses, since nothing becomes full apart from him. But see whether the one who speaks can respond to these things in this way: that, just as through the great relation and communion of the Son with rational beings the Son of God is, as it were, the fullness of all rational beings, so also he himself, as it were, takes up a fullness into himself, being shown to be most full in each of the blessed. And so that what is said may become clearer, consider a king who is filled with his kingship in each of those who increase the kingdom, but emptied of it in those who fall away; […]

And he has subjected all things under his feet, and has given him as head over the whole Church, which is his body and fullness, who is fulfilled all in all. He says that the Father has subjected the whole creation to the Son, so that, because he made all things through him (John 1:3), he himself may be the head and Lord of all. He subjected all things to him then, when he begot him before all things, so that through him he might make the things that were not. In saying the whole Church, he comprehends in sum all that is in heaven and on earth, so that they may be made his members into a new man, while they confess that he is the one through whom they were made by God. For they are subjected to him as members to the head from which they draw their origin, so that all things may be fulfilled in all. For when they have returned to the confession of the one God, bending the knee to Christ, it is fulfilled in all that he may be all; […]

"And He put all things in subjection under His feet."

Not simply so set Him above them as to be honored above them, nor by way of comparison with them, but so that He should sit over them as His slaves. Amazing! Awful indeed are these things; every created power hath been made the slave of man by reason of God the Word dwelling in Him. For it is possible for a man to be above others, without having others in subjection, but only as preferred before them. But here it is not so. No, "He put all things in subjection under His feet." And not simply put them in subjection, but in the most abject subjection, that below which there can be none. Therefore he adds, "under His feet."

"And gave Him to be Head over all things to the Church."

Amazing again, whither hath He raised the Church? as though he were lifting it up by some engine, he hath raised it up to a vast height, and set it on yonder throne; for where the Head is, there is the body also. There is no interval to separate between the Head and the body; […]

And he has subjected all things under his feet, and has given him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body: the fullness of him who is filled all in all.

This seems to be contradicted by what is written elsewhere: For we do not yet see all things subjected to him. And also by this: For he must reign until he puts all enemies under his feet (1 Cor. 15:25). For if all things are not yet subjected to him, and he must reign until all things are subjected to him, how has God now subjected the universe under his feet? Especially since Paul himself also testifies in another place: But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also will be subjected to him who subjected all things to himself, that God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28)? Therefore either, according to foreknowledge, he mentions what is going to be as though it had already been done, in the sense we expounded above, where he says: He has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ. […]

To this sense is also fitted what follows: And has given him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body. For just as a head has very many members subjected to it, some of which are faulty and weak, so also our Lord Jesus Christ, since he is the head of the Church, has as his members all those who are gathered in the Church, namely saints as well as sinners: but the saints subjected to him by will, the sinners by necessity. And so it comes about that even enemies are subjected under his feet. Wherefore, in saying all things, he seems to raise a question. For that which was said: Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet (Ps. 109:1), and elsewhere: For he must reign until he puts all enemies under his feet (1 Cor. 15:25), does not greatly require an interpreter, namely that the things which are hostile, once they have been overcome, are subjected under his feet and pass into the power of the victor. […]

But this too which he says, And has given him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body: the fullness of him who is filled all in all, can be understood of a Church not of men only, but also of angels and of all the virtues and rational creatures. Moreover this, Who is filled all in all, is by no means to be taken as it sounds; for he does not say, "Who fills all in all", but, who is filled all in all. For to fill is one thing, to be filled another; because in the one the verb belongs to the one acting, in the other to the one acted upon. Just as, then, an emperor is filled if his army is increased daily, and new provinces are made, and the multitude of his peoples grows, so also our Lord Jesus Christ, in that all things believe in him and come day by day to faith in him, is himself filled in all: yet in such a way that he is filled all in all, that is, that those who believe in him are full of all virtues, and, according to the Gospel, make him advance in age, wisdom and grace, not only with God but […]

Lest from the words "having seated above" you conclude that He received only the first honor, he indicates that He also made Him lord over all. And He did not simply subject, but gave in complete subjection: "under His feet."

O wonder! He seated the Church on that very same throne as well; because where the head is (i.e. Christ), there is the body also (i.e. the Church itself). The words "above all" indicate that He gave a head that is mighty, which is above all, above angels, above archangels.

1:23.t: Accordingly, ourselves "who were sometime alienated and enemies in our mind by wicked works" does He reconcile to the Creator, against whom we had committed offence-worshipping the creature to the prejudice of the Creator. As, however, he says elsewhere, that the Church is the body of Christ, so here also (the apostle) declares that he "fills up that which is behind of the afflictions of Christ in his flesh for His body's sake, which is the Church.

Therefore, if he bids us "be made dead to the law through the body of Christ," (which is the Church, which consists in the spirit of newness,) not "through the letter of oldness," (that is, of the law,)-taking you away from the law, which does not keep a wife, when her husband is dead, from becoming (wife) to another husband-he reduces you to (subjection to) the contrary condition, that you are not to marry when you have lost your husband; and in as far as you would not be accounted an adulteress if you became (wife) to a second husband after the death of your (first) husband, if you were still bound to act in (subjection to) the law, in so far as a result of the diversity of (your) condition, he does prejudge you (guilty) of adultery if, after the death of your husband, you do marry another: inasmuch as you have now been made dead to the law, it cannot be lawful for you, now that you have withdrawn from that (law) in the eye of which it was lawful for you.

So, then, brethren, if we do the will of our Father God, we shall be members of the first church, the spiritual, — that which was created before sun and moon; but if we shall not do the will of the Lord, we shall come under the Scripture which says, "My house became a den of robbers." [Jeremiah 7:11] So, then, let us elect to belong to the church of life, that we may be saved. I think not that you are ignorant that the living church is the body of Christ (for the Scripture, says, "God created man male and female;" [Genesis 1:27; cf. Ephesians 5:22-23] the male is Christ, the female the church,) and that the Books and the Apostles teach that the church is not of the present, but from the beginning. For it was spiritual, as was also our Jesus, and was made manifest at the end of the days in order to save you. [1 Peter 1:20]

"Which is His body."

In order then that when you hear of the Head you may not conceive the notion of supremacy only, but also of consolidation, and that you may behold Him not as supreme Ruler only, but as Head of a body.

"The fulness of Him that filleth all in all" he says.

As though this were not sufficient to show the close connection and relationship, what does he add? "The fullness of Christ is the Church." And rightly, for the complement of the head is the body, and the complement of the body is the head. Mark what great arrangement Paul observes, how he spares not a single word, that he may represent the glory of God. "The, complement," he says, i.e., the head is, as it were, filled up by the body, because the body is composed and made up of all its several parts, and he introduces Him as having need of each single one and not only of all in common and together; for unless we be many, and one be the hand, and another the foot, and another some other member, the whole body is not filled up. […]

There follows: The fullness of him who is filled all in all. This is indeed to be taken in the same way as that other saying: Then he will be subjected to him who subjected all things to himself, that God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28). For now God is in individuals in parts: in one as righteousness, in another as chastity, in another as temperance, in another as wisdom, in another as fortitude; and it is difficult, even in holy and perfect men, for all the virtues to be present equally. But when, at the end of things and the consummation of the world, the universe has been subjected to him, he will be filled all in all: so that, in accordance with the fact that God is full of all virtues, he may be filled all in all, and all may have all the things which before they possessed one by one, each his own.

By the church he means the whole community of the faithful. This he calls the body of Christ and the fullness of the Father. This body he has filled with all gifts. He "lives in it and goes about in it," as the voice of prophecy says. But this will be more strictly so in the future life.… In the present life God is in all, since his nature is uncircumscribed; but he is not "all in all," since some are impious and some lawless. Yet he lives in those who fear him and who put hope in his mercy. In the next life at any rate, when mortality has ceased and immortality is conferred and sin has no place any longer, he will be all in all.
1:23.s: Interpretation of the Epistle to the Ephesians 1.23

1:23.t: Lest you, having heard this, should think that by the name "head" some rule and authority is meant (for the word "head" has this meaning as well), he says that Christ is the head of the Church as a body, and is likewise akin to it and closely united with it. And the Church is His fullness. For just as the body is the fullness of the head, completing it with its members, so also the Church is the fullness of Christ, "who fills all in all." For Christ is completed and, as it were, perfected by all the members in the person of all believers: He is completed, as it were, by a hand in the person of a merciful man who helps the weak in various ways; He is completed, as it were, by a foot in the person of a man who undertakes a journey for the sake of preaching and who cares for his brethren, and He is completed by another member in another believer. […]

2:1.t: I suppose, forsooth, we find Him, when he speaks of such as "were dead in trespasses and sins, wherein they had walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, who worketh in the children of disobedience." But Marcion must not here interpret the world as meaning the God of the world.

Clearly sins are said to be the death of the soul, from the phrase and you, being dead in your trespasses and your sins. And since 'trespass' is a term proper to Scripture, we must examine whether it differs from 'sin,' especially since here it is said in combination: and you, being dead in your trespasses and your sins. And we inquire whether the things already wickedly accomplished by us are called our 'sins,' while the beginnings of these—being, as it were, not yet falls, but on their way toward our actually falling—are 'trespasses.' And perhaps for this reason it is said in the eighteenth Psalm, "Who shall understand trespasses?", because the one who understands the roots and beginnings of sins, which are 'trespasses,' would be able also to guard himself against falling into 'sins' as well.

The sequence is: And you, being dead in your trespasses and your sins, God made alive together with Christ, being rich in mercy through his great love with which he loved us; and being, us, dead in the trespasses, in which we once walked according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the authority of the air, of the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience, among whom we all also once conducted ourselves in the desires of our flesh, doing the wishes of the flesh and of the thoughts, and were by nature children of wrath—he made alive together with Christ. As for the connective of the passage, but God, being rich in mercy, we consider either to have been inserted pointlessly in the copies, or, as coming from Paul who was "unskilled in speech", not to have been perceived as superfluous.

And you, when you were dead in your offenses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world. He calls them dead because they follow the errors of the world; for whatever withdraws from the profession of the one God is held to be dead, because it does not remain in the root from which it draws its origin.

There is, we know, a corporal, and there is also a spiritual, dying. Of the first it is no crime to partake, nor is there any peril in it, inasmuch as there is no blame attached to it, for it is a matter of nature, not of deliberate choice. It had its origin in the transgression of the first-created man, and thenceforward in its issue it passed into a nature, and, at all events, will quickly be brought to a termination; whereas this spiritual dying, being a matter of deliberate choice, has criminality, and has no termination.

You observe the gentleness of Paul, and how on all occasions he encourages the hearer, not bearing too hard upon him. For whereas he had said, Ye have arrived at the very last degree of wickedness, (for such is the meaning of becoming dead,) that he may not excessively distress them, (because men are put to shame when their former misdeeds are brought forward, cancelled though they be, and no longer attended with danger,) he gives them, as it were, an accomplice, that it may not be supposed that the work is all their own, and that accomplice a powerful one. And who then is this? The Devil.

Now, that sin is called the death of the soul is plain from his saying, And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in accordance also with what is written in Ezekiel: The soul that sins, it shall die (Ezek. 18:4). And since trespasses (delicta), which in Greek are called παραπτώματα, is properly, according to the etymology of that same language, a word of the Scriptures (although delicta would more correctly be translated πλημμέλιαι, "offences"), we ask what they signify, and in what they differ from sins, that is, what difference there is between παραπτώματα and ἁμαρτίας. For they say that παραπτώματα are, as it were, the beginnings of sins, when a thought creeps in silently and, though we connive in some measure, has not yet driven us to ruin. Hence also in the eighteenth psalm (v. 13) it is written: Trespasses, that is, παραπτώματα, who understands?, namely because it is difficult to understand the roots and beginnings of sins. […]

And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now works in the sons of unbelief, in which we also all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the wills of the flesh and of the thoughts, and were by nature sons of wrath, even as the rest. But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ.

Before we discuss the senses of the individual words, it seems to us that the order of the reading should be rendered thus: And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins, God, who is rich in mercy, made alive together with Christ, because of his great love with which he loved us; […]

Above he said that God manifested in us the same power and working as in Christ. Of Him it is said that He raised Him from the dead and seated Him above all. And then now he speaks also of us: "and you," he says, "who were dead" (not by bodily death, which began with Adam, but by the death of the soul, which comes from ourselves, the death of sin) He raised and lifted up. So then, by the same power He both raised the Lord from bodily death and us from the spiritual death of sin, and the transformation of the soul's disposition is far more important than the raising of the dead, as was said above. The thought of this passage is indeed such, but it is stretched out too much until the words "made alive together with Christ," since much has been inserted and there is repetition in the words "God, who is rich in mercy." […]

2:2.t: If any one confesses the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost, and praises the creation, but calls the incarnation merely an appearance, and is ashamed of the passion, such an one has denied the faith, not less than the Jews who killed Christ. If any one confesses these things, and that God the Word did dwell in a human body, being within it as the Word, even as the soul also is in the body, because it was God that inhabited it, and not a human soul, but affirms that unlawful unions are a good thing, and places the highest happiness in pleasure, as does the man who is falsely called a Nicolaitan, this person can neither be a lover of God, nor a lover of Christ, but is a corrupter of his own flesh, and therefore void of the Holy Spirit, and a stranger to Christ. All such persons are but monuments and sepulchres of the dead, upon which are written only the names of dead men. […]
2:2.s: Epistle of Ignatius to the Philadelphians

2:2.t: They are ashamed of the cross; they mock at the passion; they make a jest of the resurrection. They are the offspring of that spirit who is the author of all evil, who led Adam, by means of his wife, to transgress the commandment, who slew Abel by the hands of Cain, who fought against Job, who was the accuser of Joshua the son of Josedech, who sought to "sift the faith" of the apostles, who stirred up the multitude of the Jews against the Lord, who also now "worketh in the children of disobedience; from whom the Lord Jesus Christ will deliver us, who prayed that the faith of the apostles might not fail, not because He was not able of Himself to preserve it, but because He rejoiced in the pre-eminence of the Father. It is fitting, therefore, that ye should keep aloof from such persons, and neither in private nor in public to talk with them; but to give heed to the law, and the prophets, and to those who have preached to you the word of salvation. […]
2:2.s: Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans

2:2.t: And indeed, before the cross was erected, he (Satan) was eager that it should be so; and he "wrought" [for this end] "in the children of disobedience." He wrought in Judas, in the Pharisees, in the Sadducees, in the old, in the young, and in the priests. But when it was just about to be erected, he was troubled, and infused repentance into the traitor, and pointed him to a rope to hang himself with, and taught him [to die by] strangulation. He terrified also the silly woman, disturbing her by dreams; and he, who had tried every means to have the cross prepared, now endeavoured to put a stop to its erection; not that he was influenced by repentance on account of the greatness of his crime (for in that case he would not be utterly depraved), but because he perceived his own destruction [to be at hand]. For the cross of Christ was the beginning of his condemnation the beginning of his death, the beginning of his destruction. […]
2:2.s: Epistle of Pseudo-Ignatius to the Philippians

2:2.t: Just as if any one, being an apostate, and seizing in a hostile manner another man's territory, should harass the inhabitants of it, in order that he might claim for himself the glory of a king among those ignorant of his apostasy and robbery; so likewise also the devil, being one among those angels who are placed over the spirit of the air, as the Apostle Paul has declared in his Epistle to the Ephesians, becoming envious of man, was rendered an apostate from the divine law: for envy is a thing foreign to God. And as his apostasy was exposed by man, and man became the [means of] searching out his thoughts (et examinatio sententiae ejus, homo factus est), he has set himself to this with greater and greater determination, in opposition to man, envying his life, and wishing to involve him in his own apostate power. The Word of God, however, the Maker of all things, conquering him by means of human nature, and showing him to be an apostate, has, on the contrary, put him under the power of man. […]

What is it to walk according to the age of this world, and not according to the age of the better world toward which the saints hasten? Now one person will, more simply, hold the age of this world to be the time coextensive with the constitution of this world from beginning to end. But another, from what follows, will suspect whether perhaps the ruler of the authority of the air, of the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience, is the same as the age of this world, since all these things are set down as though of one entity, Paul saying, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the authority of the air, of the spirit; […]

And it must be observed that he did not say 'according to the ruler of the air' but 'of the authority of the air'; therefore we must inquire into the authority of the air, that thus we may see the ruler of it. But the wording can also indicate something like this: according to the ruler of the authority, of the spirit—which spirit is the spirit of the air—that now works in the sons of disobedience. Since, then, the ruler is ruler of something, you will consider whether the one now spoken of is ruler of every authority concerning the air, which works, dwelling about the air, upon the sons of disobedience (and everyone who, when divine doctrines are proclaimed, disobeys them, by the very act of disobeying shows himself to be a son of disobedience); and consider whether "our wrestling" is against "these authorities", as we resist the workings which they wish to produce in us as well, wishing to make us sons of disobedience. […]

Where our Lord Jesus Christ, who took upon Him to die for all, stretched forth His hands, not somewhere on the earth beneath, but in the air itself, in order that the Salvation effected by the Cross might be shewn to be for all men everywhere: destroying the devil who was working in the air: and that He might consecrate our road up to Heaven, and make it free.

According to the prince of the power of this air, the spirit that now works in the sons of distrust. By the prince of the power, that is, the devil, he signifies that he corrupted the understanding of the world, so that they withdrew from the one God, taking up the opinion of many gods, in order that he might make them companions of his conspiracy, while they are found in the same ungodliness, denying the one God. He calls this prince of error, then, the spirit of the air for this reason: to show that he usurped this region for himself for the exercise of dominion. For the air is one thing and the prince another: but because he holds dominion in the world or in the air, he is called the spirit of the air.

Let us, therefore, fear the judgment which awaits teachers. For a severe judgment will those teachers receive "who teach, but do not," and those who take upon them the name of Christ falsely, and say: We teach the truth, and yet go wandering about idly, and exalt themselves, and make their boast "in the mind of the flesh." These, moreover, are like "the blind man who leads the blind man, and they both fall into the ditch." [Matthew 15:14] And they will receive judgment, because in their talkativeness and their frivolous teaching they teach natural wisdom and the "frivolous error of the plausible words of the wisdom of men," "according to the will of the prince of the dominion of the air, and of the spirit which works in those men who will not obey, according to the training of this world, and not according to the doctrine of Christ." […]

Why does he call the Devil "the prince" of the world? Because nearly the whole human race has surrendered itself to him and all are willingly and of deliberate choice his slaves. And to Christ, though He promises unnumbered blessings, not any one so much as gives any heed; whilst to the Devil, though promising nothing of the sort, but sending them on to hell, all yield themselves. His kingdom then is in this world, and he has, with few exceptions, more subjects and more obedient subjects than God, in consequence of our indolence.

"According to the power," saith he, "of the air, of the spirit." Here again he means, that Satan occupies the space under Heaven, and that the incorporeal powers are spirits of the air, under his operation. For that his kingdom is of this age, i. e., will cease with the present age, hear what he says at the end of the Epistle; "Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities, against powers, against the world rulers of this darkness;" where, lest when you hear of world-rulers you should therefore say that the Devil is uncreated, he elsewhere calls a perverse time, "an evil world," not of the creatures. For he seems to me, having had dominion beneath the sky, not to have fallen from his dominion, even after his transgression.

"That now worketh," he says, "in the sons of disobedience." You observe that it is not by force, nor by compulsion, but by persuasion, he wins us over; "disobedience" or "untractableness" is his word, as though one were to say, by guile and persuasion he draws all his votaries to himself.

We also ask what is meant by in which you once walked according to the age of this world: whether there is also another age, which does not belong to this world but to other worlds, of which Clement too writes in his Epistle: "Ocean, and the worlds which are beyond it"? Or whether this is the one world, which rolls on from the beginning of the age in which Adam was made until its end, and passes away; or whether, surely, the prince of this air, who now works in the sons of unbelief, is called by the other name "world"? It is also written to the Galatians: That he might deliver us from the present evil age (Gal. 1:4). And in this same Epistle: Redeeming the time, because the days are evil (below, 5:16). And the days of Jacob are called few and evil (Gen. 47), whether because the time of this life, through which we are held shut in the age, is heavy and laborious, or because Satan himself, as we said above, is called by the name of this world and of the age. […]

Long ago, before the Fall, a certain authority was primordially entrusted to the devil. But falling from this through wickedness he became a teacher of impiety and wickedness. Yet he does not have power over all but only over those who do not receive divine revelation. These Paul calls "sons of disobedience."
2:2.s: Interpretation of the Epistle to the Ephesians 2.1-2

2:2.t: the divine Apostle, speaking of the Adversary, teaches what was his work from the beginning in these words: According to the prince of the power of the air, of the spirit that now worketh in the sons of disobedience —words which clearly show him to have been formerly a prince endowed with the power of moving the air and changing its place, but one now cast out for ever from this dignity; yea, rather, one who from sheer depravity works upon sinners, as is evident from the fact that he stood not alone in having the power to do this, but shared it in common with many others. For some of the angels were commissioned to move the air, some the sun, some the moon, some the stars, while others prepared the clouds and the rains, and rendered many other services— for this is the work, the appointed duty, of the angelic orders and powers—to minister to the well-being and honour of the image of God, that is, of man, and to move all things like soldiers obeying the commands of the king. […]

You sinned, thus, "according to the course of this world," that is, thinking about worldly and temporal things and making bad use of this age. For this age is not evil, but the misuse of it is. It was given as a guide, since, being corruptible and quickly passing, it can arouse us toward the incorruptible and unchanging; but we, having given ourselves over to its corruption and flux, made it not a guide but an opponent. By "prince" who "has dominion in the air," he means the devil, and not the Demiurge, as the impious Manichaeans think. He calls him "prince" because people have subjected themselves to him and serve him more than God. However, such power of his exists only in this age and does not extend beyond the air, because it has place not in heaven but under heaven. Therefore Paul also calls him the prince "who has dominion in the air," not in the sense that he rules over the air and controls it, but because he loves to dwell in it. […]

2:3.t: " In perfect agreement with reason was that indignation which resulted from his desire to maintain discipline and order. When, however, he says, "We were formerly the children of wrath," he censures an irrational irascibility, such as proceeds not from that nature which is the production of God, but from that which the devil brought in, who is himself styled the lord or "master" of his own class, "Ye cannot serve two masters," and has the actual designation of "father: ""Ye are of your father the devil.

" And if so, the apostle too was in error when he said in his epistle, "Ye were at one time darkness, (but now are ye light in the Lord: )" and, "We also were by nature children of wrath; " and, "Such were some of you, but ye are washed.

But the apostle, too, had lived in Judaism; and when he parenthetically observed of the sins (of that period of his life), "in which also we all had our conversation in times past," he must not be understood to indicate that the Creator was the lord of sinful men, and the prince of this air; but as meaning that in his Judaism he had been one of the children of disobedience, having the devil as his instigator-when he persecuted the church and the Christ of the Creator.

But the apostle, too, had lived in Judaism; and when he parenthetically observed of the sins (of that period of his life), "in which also we all had our conversation in times past," he must not be understood to indicate that the Creator was the lord of sinful men, and the prince of this air; but as meaning that in his Judaism he had been one of the children of disobedience, having the devil as his instigator-when he persecuted the church and the Christ of the Creator. Therefore he says: "We also were the children of wrath," but "by nature." Let the heretic, however, not contend that, because the Creator called the Jews children, therefore the Creator is the lord of wrath.

For when (the apostle) says," We were by nature the children of wrath," inasmuch as the Jews were not the Creator's children by nature, but by the election of their fathers, he (must have) referred their being children of wrath to nature, and not to the Creator, adding this at lasts" even as others," who, of course, were not children of God.

Similarly, too, (when writing) to the Ephesians, while recalling past (deeds), he warns (them) concerning the future: "In which we too had our conversation, doing the concupiscences and pleasures of the flesh." Branding, in fine, such as had denied themselves-Christians, to wit-on the score of having "delivered themselves up to the working of every impunity," "But ye," he says, "not so have learnt Christ.

But the phrase and among whom we all also once conducted ourselves—among what things, if not the trespasses? For indeed he assigned nothing to correspond to the trespasses, but only to the sins; having said, at any rate, and you, being dead in your trespasses and your sins, he adds in which you once walked; but now he assigns, to correspond to your trespasses, the phrase and among which we all also once conducted ourselves, lest, having said in which you once walked according to the age of this world while keeping silent about himself, he should seem, as it were, to be boasting. But Paul himself knows a certain desire of the flesh, and another desire of the spirit, saying "the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh".

And having conducted ourselves in the trespasses, since we were in the desires of our flesh, we did not one thing but many wishes, and not only of the flesh but also of the thoughts; and we inquire what the wishes of the thoughts are, being other than the wishes of the flesh; and we conjecture that, on the one hand, by doing the works of the flesh and loving pleasure one does the wishes of the flesh, while, on the other, by having fallen away from sound opinion and right thinking we do the wishes of the thoughts.

But as to the phrase we were by nature children of wrath, as also the rest, we do not know what those will ever say who introduce spiritual natures from the beginning; for how the one who is by nature Son of God is said to be by nature a son of wrath, let them answer. But we suppose that it was because of the "body of humiliation" that we became children by nature of wrath, when "our thought lay upon evil things from youth"; for according to Solomon, "there is no righteous person upon the earth who will do good and will not sin".

For if we examine the matter more fully, we shall show that those who are now righteous were previously unrighteous, but, having applied themselves, they were changed. For Abraham himself is read to have been justified by faith (James 2:23 and Rom. 4:3). Therefore, before this he was not righteous, since he is understood to have worshipped idols under the guidance of his father. And Zacchaeus too, to whom after a common sort of life the Lord bears witness (Luke 19:9). And the vessel of election, who also admits this, saying, “We too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3); because the will yields superiority over nature. For one is judged by the will, not by nature. Without doubt all the martyrs and the righteous became good; for they were not born faithful, but reborn. And how many do we know to have lived a shameful life, extravagant devotees of luxury, who are now self-controlled and holy? For when the fear of God draws near, the vices that once ruled are overcome.
2:3.s: QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 115: CONCERNING FATE

2:3.t: In which we too once had our way of life in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of its counsels: and we were by nature sons of wrath, even as the rest. He signifies faithlessness when he mentions the desires of the flesh. For the will of the flesh is to take delight in visible things, so that it calls gods the elements which God established as the helms of the world; whereas this name is owed to the one God, from whom are all things, so that just as he has no partner among these in power, so he may have no sharer in the name. But this name is not denied to Christ for this reason: because just as their nature is common, so too will the name be. Yet there is this difference between the Father and the Son, that the Father received this from no one, while the Son received all that is the Father's through generation, so that in power and substance and name the Son differs in nothing from the Father. Hence he says: All things that the Father has are mine; and mine are the Father's (John 16:15). […]

The divine Scripture knows how to use the word "Son" in both senses, so that in some cases such an appellation is derived from nature, in others it is adventitious and artificial. For when it speaks of "sons of men," or "sons of rams," it marks the essential relation of that which is begotten to that from which it has its being: but when it speaks of "sons of power," or "children of God," it presents to us that kinship which is the result of choice. And, moreover, in the opposite sense, too, the same persons are called "sons of Eli," and "sons of Belial," the appellation of "sons" being easily adapted to either idea. For when they are called "sons of Eli," they are declared to have natural relationship to him, but in being called "sons of Belial," they are reproved for the wickedness of their choice, as no longer emulating their father in their life, but addicting their own purpose to sin. […]

"In the lusts of our flesh, doing the desires of the flesh, and of the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest." That is, having no spiritual affections. Yet, lest he should slander the flesh, or lest it should be supposed that the transgression was not great, observe how he guards the matter, "Doing," he says, "the desires of the flesh and of the mind." That is, the pleasurable passions. We provoked God to anger, he saith, we provoked Him to wrath, we were wrath, and nothing else. For as he who is a child of man is by nature man, so also were we children of wrath even as others; i. e., no one was free, but we all did things worthy of wrath.

There follows: In which we also all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the wills of the flesh and of the minds. What he says, in which (in quibus), is to be referred to the trespasses. For above, since he had set down two things together, And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins, and had referred to the sins by saying, in which you once walked, while nothing of the kind seemed to have followed for the trespasses that could complete the sense, he now says: in which trespasses we also all lived; and at the same time, lest in having said, and your sins, in which you once walked, he should seem through pride to exempt himself from sin, he added, in which we also all lived. Now he who says that he has lived so is confessing past trespasses, not present ones. We lived once, he says, not in one desire, but in the desires of our flesh. For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. 5:17). Doing not one will of the flesh, but many; […]

Some, in place of what we have now expounded, And we were by nature sons of wrath, have translated, in place of by nature, "utterly" or "altogether", since the word φύσει is ambiguous. And even if it sounds so, it must be expounded according to what we have said.

Of nature itself we speak in one sense, when we properly describe it as that human nature in which man was created faultless after his kind; and in another sense as that nature in which we are born ignorant and carnally minded, owing to the penalty of condemnation, after the manner of the apostle, "We ourselves likewise were by nature children of wrath, even as others."

Accordingly, the Apostle Paul, in a certain passage, having both conditions in view,—even the wrath of God with which we are born, and the grace whereby we are delivered,—says: "Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others. But God, who is rich in mercy, for His great love wherewith He loved us, even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ; by whose grace we are saved." What, then, is man's "natural malice," and "the seed cursed from the beginning;" and what are "the natural brute beasts made to be taken and destroyed," and what the "by nature children of wrath"? Was this the condition of the nature which was formed in Adam? God forbid!
